# Board Doc Render Test

This page is a test fixture for `site/scripts/check-rendered-docs.mjs`. Its blocks are copied from the whitepaper's Part 1 as the board wrote them, so the renderer is tested on real board output: two PlotCharts, a Carousel of four, two figure frames, inline notes of several paragraphs, a table and an image.

A felt minute counts how long each minute feels: a minute walking or waiting feels like 1.75 minutes riding.^[Wardman and others, 2026, via our resources note: parking search 1.6, driving in traffic 1.33, riding 1. Their mean weights are 1.67 for walking and 1.72 for waiting, and the review supports "1.75 or 1.50", so we use 1.75. [primary — read 2026-11-13, per repo note] Bike riding at 1, unlocking a bike at 1.75, and 1.75 for a whole trip on foot are our own extensions. [inference — mine]] Bars show felt minutes and the black tick clock minutes, with Muni buses at 8.8 mph ([Muni page](https://sf-works.org/transportation/muni)), cars at 13.3 mph and bikes at 9 mph.^[Muni: citywide bus speed from 511 stop observations over the last 365 days, at the hours the car trips ran, 7 to 10 a.m. and 1 to 4 p.m. [511 historic stop observations, via site/data/muni.json — read 2026-11-14] Cars: Google's door-to-door times with traffic for 73 SF trips of 2 to 4 miles departing Tuesday 2026-10-13. Minutes over Google's no-traffic time count as driving in traffic. Bikes: Google's median on 100 SF school trips. [Google Routes API — queried 2026-10-08] The walk to and from the stop, 5.4 and 4.1 minutes, is the median over our transit model's zone pairs. [per repo note — read 2026-11-14]] We count the wait as half the gap between buses, assume 3 minutes hunting for parking, and leave out transfers, crowding and late buses.^[Also assumed: a 1-minute walk to the car, 2 minutes from it, 1 minute unlocking a bike at each end, and walking at 3 mph. [inference — mine] Liao and others assume parking adds "a random value between 5 and 10 minutes" ([Liao 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-61077-0)), so our 5 is their low end. SFpark found cruising on metered blocks took "just a few seconds" ([Millard-Ball and others](https://www.cmu.edu/traffic21/pdfs/millard-ball_weinberger_hampshire_2014_assessing_the_impacts_sfpark-compressed.pdf)). Wardman finds riders time their arrival on infrequent lines, so the 20-minute bar runs high. [primary — read 2026-11-13, per repo note]]

This counts trips to work only. In 2025, 38% of San Francisco workers went to work by car, up from 35% in 2019 and a low of 32% in 2021, when almost half of us worked from home.^[US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-year estimates, table B08301, 2010 to 2025, for [San Francisco](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2025.B08301?g=050XX00US06075), [Seattle](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2025.B08301?g=160XX00US5363000) and [Boston](https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2025.B08301?g=160XX00US2507000). [primary — read 2026-11-13] ¶ Driving alone only, 2010 to 2025: San Francisco 36% to 33%, Seattle 53% to 41%, Boston 38% to 31%. ¶ These are shares. Fewer San Franciscans work than in 2019, so the number going by car, about 174,000 in 2025, is close to 2019's 184,000. Each year's share is good to within 1 to 2 points either way.] Seattle and Boston are still below their 2019 shares, and there's no 2020 point because the Census didn't publish one.
